title: [CuTe, SM90] Skip the causal/local mask on unmasked KV blocks in forward
body:
### Motivation

On H200 the FA4 SM90 causal forward trails the C++ FA3 forward by 8-20% at every sequence length, while the non-causal forward is at parity. Fitting kernel time against `seqlen_k` shows the per-KV-block cost of the *non-causal* kernels is identical (FA3 1.626 us vs FA4 1.620 us per block per SM), so the causal gap has to come from the causal kernel itself.

### Cause

The SM90 mainloop splits the KV iterations into blocks that need masking (the diagonal, or the window edges for local) and blocks that do not. The second loop ("The remaining iterations have no masking") still passes `mask_fn`, which is bound with `mask_causal=self.is_causal` / `mask_local=self.is_local`. So every unmasked block re-applies the causal mask element-wise, even though it is all-true there. In the SASS of the hdim-128 causal kernel the unmasked inner loop has 580 instructions with 66 `FSEL` and 8 `R2P`, against 457 instructions / 2 `FSEL` / 0 `R2P` in the non-causal kernel.

`flash_fwd_sm100.py` already handles this loop correctly: it only passes `mask_fn` when `mask_mod` is set. This PR does the same on SM90. With the change the unmasked inner loop drops to 477 instructions, 2 `FSEL`, 0 `R2P`; the masked loop is unchanged.

### Performance (H200, bf16, `benchmarks`-style shapes with 32k total tokens, CUDA-event timing)

| forward | FA3 | FA4 main | FA4 this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| hdim128 causal 1k | 509 | 414 | 431 |
| hdim128 causal 4k | 691 | 607 | 643 |
| hdim128 causal 8k | 679 | 637 | 667 |
| hdim128 causal 16k | 682 | 613 | **660** |
| hdim64 causal 4k | 481 | 410 | 466 |
| hdim64 causal 16k | 514 | 463 | **531** |
| hdim128 non-causal 16k | 685 | 665 | 665 |

TFLOPS. Non-causal is untouched (same kernel). The remaining gap at short sequence lengths is the single-tile (non-persistent) scheduler on SM90, which is a separate issue (#2754 territory).

### Correctness

- Forward `out` and `lse` are bitwise identical to main for 9 configurations: causal with sq==sk, sq<sk, sq>sk, GQA, hdim 64/128/192/256, local windows (256,0) and (300,100), and non-causal.
- `tests/cute/test_flash_attn_fast.py` + a `test_flash_attn.py` subset (sm90 hdim padding, small head dim, pack_gqa, lse_grad, `test_flash_attn_output` at 113x203 / 1024x1023 / 4224x4224): 2010 passed; the 4 failures are the same `dSink` tolerance failures as on main.
- `tests/cute/test_mask_mod.py`: 1256 passed, 120 failed, the identical set as main (fixed by #2903).
- `tests/cute/test_flash_attn_varlen.py -k "2048 and dtype0"`: 972 passed, 0 failed.

All test runs on H200 with the compile cache disabled or in a fresh cache dir.

title: [CuTe, SM90] Fit forward tile to the block-sparse block size
body:
### Motivation

`flash_attn_func` / `flash_attn_varlen_func` (and flex attention's FLASH backend, which calls them) take no tile sizes. On SM90 the forward tile comes from `_tile_size_fwd_sm90`, which only adjusts `tile_m` for the sparse Q block when head_dim <= 96. It never looks at the sparse KV block. SM90 has no KV subtiling (`kv_subtile_factor` must be 1), and a sparse Q block smaller than `tile_m` cannot be subtiled either. So any `BlockSparseTensorsTorch.block_size` that differs from the heuristic tile raises a `ValueError` in the forward, even when the kernel runs that tile fine through `_flash_attn_fwd(..., tile_mn=...)`:

- hdim 192: flex's default `BLOCK_SIZE=128` fails (`tile_n=112`).
- hdim 256: every KV block except 80 fails (`tile_n=80`). The only accepted size, (128, 80), is then rejected by the backward (`tile_n=64`), so SM90 hdim-256 block sparsity through autograd is not usable at all.
- hdim <= 128: (64, 128), (128, 64), (64, 64), (128, 112), ... all fail.

It also accounts for all 120 SM90 failures of `test_mask_mod.py::test_parameterized_masks[True-128-112-*]` / `[True-64-128-*]` (use_autograd=True with block sparsity). Those have failed on Hopper since the autograd variant was added in #2485. FA4 CI runs only on B200, which skips non-128x128 tiles, so nothing caught them.

### Change

`_fit_sm90_fwd_tile_to_block_sparsity` runs after the SM90 heuristic when the caller supplies `block_size`:
- If the sparse Q block isn't a multiple of `tile_m` but is a multiple of 64, use `tile_m=64`. Larger sparse Q blocks still use `q_subtile_factor`.
- If the sparse KV block is smaller than `tile_n` and a multiple of 16, use `tile_n = sparse KV block`.

The tile only shrinks, which never adds smem or register pressure. The rule fires only when the heuristic tile would already have been rejected by `normalize_block_sparse_config`, so configurations that work today are unchanged: same tiles, same kernels, same performance. Also fixes the SM90 KV-subtile error message, which printed `tile_n` where it meant the sparse KV block size.

### Results (H200, bf16, B=2 H=4 S=1024, block-aligned causal BlockMask vs fp32 flex)

(head_dim x block size) combinations accepted by `flash_attn_func`, out of 40 (hdim 64/96/128/192/256 x 8 block sizes):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| forward | 8 / 40 | 32 / 40 |
| forward + backward | 6 / 40 | 11 / 40 |

Forward max abs error vs the fp32 flex reference is <= 0.0039 for every newly accepted case. The remaining backward rejections come from the SM90 backward's own tile_n (128 for hdim <= 128, 96 for 192, 64 for 256). That is a separate heuristic and is left for a follow-up.

### Tests

- New `test_sm90_block_sparse_fwd_tile_fits_block_size` (7 cases, forward and backward where supported, via `flash_attn_func`): 7/7 fail on main, 7/7 pass here.
- `tests/cute/test_mask_mod.py` (H200): main 1256 passed / **120 failed** -> this PR **1383 passed / 0 failed** (+7 new).
- `tests/cute/test_block_sparsity.py` (H200): 4883 passed / 0 failed.
- `tests/cute/test_mask_mod_varlen.py` + `tests/cute/test_flash_attn_fast.py` (H200): 784 passed, 2 failed. The two failures, `test_varlen_static_masks[block_diagonal-mha-*]`, were CUDA OOMs while four suites shared the node. Rerun alone, they pass on both main and this PR (17/17).
- Two-pass run (`FLASH_ATTENTION_FAKE_TENSOR=1` compile, then GPU), separate cache dir for the patched tree. `ruff check`: no new findings.

This overlaps the function that #2733 moves into typed configs. The change is a self-contained post-pass and is easy to rebase onto that stack, whichever lands first.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Write real zeros for block-sparse empty tiles
body:
A Q tile with no live KV blocks skips its QK/PV sequence entirely. The PV GEMM
carries zero_init on its first iteration and is the only writer of the O
accumulator, so for an empty tile the O region in TMEM is never written --
tcgen05.alloc reserves the columns without initialising them.

The empty-tile path relied on calling correction_epilogue with scale 0.0 to
turn that residue into zeros. But 0.0 * NaN and 0.0 * Inf are both NaN, and
infinities are routine content for attention TMEM, so the tile yields zeros
most of the time and NaN whenever a prior kernel left an infinity behind.

Add a constexpr zero_fill to correction_epilogue so an empty tile fills the
fragment directly and never reads TMEM. Being constexpr, the non-empty call
site codegens exactly as before.

SM90 needs no equivalent flag: acc_O lives in registers and is already zeroed
inline in the mainloop. Forward counterpart to #2776.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Sparse MLA bwd: keep P normalization and dS product in fp32
body:
## Summary

The softmax warps of the sparse-MLA backward (`flash_bwd_mla_sm100.py`) rounded three intermediates to bf16 before forming `dS = P ⊙ (dP − dPsum) · softmax_scale`: the normalization scale `scale_p`, the normalized `P`, and `(dP − dPsum) · softmax_scale`. This PR keeps an fp32 copy of `P^T` and forms the product in fp32, rounding to bf16 exactly once for the dS store.

- **Load-P path (default):** the saved bf16 `p` is upcast, normalized with the fp32 `scale_p`, and rounded to bf16 once for the `dV += P^T·dO` mma operand; the fp32 copy is used for dS.
- **Recompute-P path (`gather_bwd_recompute_p=True`):** the fp32 `exp2` result already exists; it now stays live for dS instead of being re-read from the bf16 staging copy.
- Unchanged: forward kernel, saved activations, dS storage dtype, all mma operand dtypes, smem layout.
- `AI/SPARSE_MLA_RECOMPUTE_P.md` numerics section updated.

Both backward paths (load-P and recompute-P) get the same treatment so their dS numerics stay on one scheme.

## Validation (GB200, CUTLASS DSL 4.7.1, torch 2.14)

- `pytest tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py -k mla_sparse`: **34 passed** (sentinel, sentinel_varlen, recompute_p, fully_masked_rows, token_chunk_rect, token_chunk_varlen, learnable_sink).

The same case fails identically on unmodified `main` (e81a70c) in a standalone run, so it is pre-existing and unrelated to this change. Rerunning the other 96 `kv_sparsity=True` cases in a fresh process: **96 passed**.
- `pytest tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py -k mla_absorbed_varlen` (832 cases, all `kv_sparsity=True`): the first `seqlen_q=1, seqlen_k=4096` case hits the same illegal memory access (also reproduced standalone on unmodified `main`), taking the rest of that process down. Excluding the 128 `seqlen_q=1` cases and rerunning: **704 passed**, 0 failed.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Sparse MLA training fwd: exact running softmax max
body:
Stacked on #2893 (its commit is the first commit here; this PR's own change is the second, `65846ed`). The O-residual dpsum PR (#2908) builds on this one.

## Summary

FA4's online softmax only rescales the `O`/`row_sum` accumulators when a block's max exceeds the running max by more than `rescale_threshold = 8` (log2 units). With the stale max the row's dominant probability is `exp2(delta)` with a non-integer `delta` instead of exactly 1.0, and its bf16 rounding (the P@V MMA operand) is a coherent ~2^-9 gain error on the whole output row: the effective attention weights no longer sum to 1.

The sparse-MLA kernel processes the gathered index blocks from the last to the first, so a top-k indexer's slot 0 (the strongest key) is processed **last**, which is exactly the case where the stale max is wrong. Two consequences for training:

- peaked rows (a token attending mostly to its own key, the norm in causal DSA) carry a per-token, per-head gain error that compounds across layers and also enters the backward through `dpsum = rowsum(dO * O)`;
- the output depends on the *order* of the top-k indices: the same set in ascending order (self key last, processed first) does not show the error, any other order does.

## Change

Sparse-MLA forwards whose inputs require grad construct `FlashAttentionMLAForwardSm100` with `rescale_threshold=0` (exact running max; the dominant `p` is exactly 1.0 in bf16). Inference keeps 8. The threshold is a constructor parameter and part of the compile key; there are no user-facing knobs. Training and inference forward outputs are therefore no longer bitwise equal. Backward kernels, memory and the inference kernel are untouched (the inference build is the same binary: same registers, local memory and instruction mix).

## Accuracy

T = S = 4096, W = 2048, H = 128, bf16, fp64 reference from the same bf16 inputs, rel-L2 in absolute units (1.66e-3 = the bf16 output-rounding floor, `bf16(o_ref)` vs `o_ref`). "Row gain" = per-(token, head) `<out - o_ref, o_ref> / <o_ref, o_ref>`, the coherent component of the error. Peaked inputs: `q_t += 0.25 k_t`, `qv_t += 0.25 v_t` (median self weight 0.17, p90 0.41). FlashMLA's sparse forward on the same inputs is shown as a reference.

**Forward, same top-k set, dominant key in the last slot (processed first) vs in slot 0 (top-k order, processed last)**

| forward | ordering | out rel-L2 | row-gain rms (p99) | out diff between the two orders | coherent part of the diff / rounding-noise floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lazy max (before) | last slot | 1.67e-3 | 1.48e-4 (4.1e-4) | – | – |
| lazy max (before) | slot 0 | **2.07e-3** | **1.23e-3 (3.0e-3)** | 2.16e-3 | 1.24e-3 / 1.95e-4 = **6.4x** |
| exact max (after) | last slot | 1.67e-3 | 1.46e-4 (4.0e-4) | – | – |
| exact max (after) | slot 0 | 1.67e-3 | 1.38e-4 (3.6e-4) | 7.3e-4 | 1.14e-4 / 1.09e-4 = 1.0x |
| FlashMLA sparse fwd | last slot | 1.67e-3 | 1.79e-4 (4.8e-4) | – | – |
| FlashMLA sparse fwd | slot 0 | 1.67e-3 | 1.48e-4 (4.1e-4) | 7.8e-4 | 1.67e-4 / 1.14e-4 = 1.5x |

The elementwise difference between two orders (~7e-4) is inherent to any bf16-P online softmax (P is rounded relative to the running max at the time its block is processed) and has a grad-norm footprint of ~1e-6; only the coherent part is fixable, and the exact max removes it. iid inputs: out 2.01e-3 → 1.96e-3, row gain 2.57e-4 → 1.97e-4 (floor 1.63e-3 / 1.27e-4); FlashMLA 2.00e-3 / 2.50e-4.

**Gradients (this change alone; dpsum still from the bf16 output), rel-L2 vs fp64, dominant key in slot 0**

| inputs | fwd | dq | dqv | dk | dv |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| peaked | lazy max | 3.35e-3 | 3.27e-3 | 2.86e-3 | 2.22e-3 |
| peaked | exact max | 3.18e-3 | 3.10e-3 | 2.67e-3 | 1.85e-3 |
| iid | lazy max | 2.84e-3 | 2.51e-3 | 2.32e-3 | 2.21e-3 |
| iid | exact max | 2.80e-3 | 2.48e-3 | 2.27e-3 | 2.15e-3 |

With the exact max the gradients no longer depend on the index order (last slot vs slot 0 agree to three digits; before: 3.18e-3 vs 3.35e-3).

## Cost

GB200, T = S = 16K, W = 2048, H = 128, load-P, CUDA-event timing, same GPU back-to-back (mean of 2 runs):

| | fwd (train) ms | bwd ms | fwd+bwd ms | peak extra GiB | saved activations GiB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 8.74 | 33.05 | 40.74 | 20.55 | 12.53 |
| after | 9.05 (+3.6%) | 33.05 | 40.81 (+0.2%) | 20.55 | 12.53 |

Inference forward: 7.67 vs 7.63 ms (unchanged, same binary). For reference, FlashMLA's sparse forward is ~1.4x faster than FA4's at equal head count in a separate benchmark (6.2 vs 8.6 ms at 16K, 128 heads); this PR does not change that gap materially.

## Tests

- New `test_flash_attn_mla_sparse_topk_order_invariance` (causal × bf16): same set with the dominant key first and last; asserts the coherent component of the difference is < 2x the rounding-noise floor, each ordering is < 2x the ideal bf16 row gain, and the gradient rel-L2 vs fp64 is order-independent within 5%. Forcing `rescale_threshold = 8` fails it with a 7–10x margin. Passes in fake and real mode.
- Adds the fp64 sparse-MLA reference and the self-including top-k index helper the test needs (also used by the follow-up PR).
- All 36 `mla_sparse` tests (34 existing + these 2) pass in fake and real mode.

Design notes: `AI/SPARSE_MLA_EXACT_SOFTMAX_MAX.md`. It also records an alternative that was measured but not adopted here (accumulating `row_sum` over the bf16-rounded P: same accuracy on the output, ~3% faster forward from fewer spills, but changes what `lse` means and touches the inference and fp8 paths).

title: [CuTe, SM100] Sparse MLA training: dpsum from an O residual
body:
Stacked on #2893 and on the exact-softmax-max PR #2907 (their commits are the first three here; this PR's own change is the fourth, `9e523af`).

## Summary

The softmax backward forms `dS = P * (dP - dpsum)` with `dpsum = rowsum(dO * O)`. The backward only has the bf16 output, and whenever a row's attention is peaked (one key carries most of the weight, the norm in causal DSA) `dP ~ dpsum` on the dominant key: the small difference of two large numbers is dominated by the bf16 rounding of `O`, which is coherent along the row and so does not average out in the dot product with `dO`. That error lands on the dominant key's `dS` and propagates coherently into dq and dk.

A stage-by-stage fp64 error decomposition of the sparse-MLA training path (`AI/SPARSE_MLA_DPSUM_PRECISION.md`) shows every kernel is fp32-accurate for its own inputs; the gap to fp64 is bf16 rounding, and this one term is avoidable and dominant for peaked rows: at ~80% self-attention weight dq/dk rel-L2 vs fp64 is 0.89% with ~1% of rows at ~100% error, identically in load-P and recompute-P mode and in an emulated dense bf16 pipeline that forms dpsum from bf16 O. At 97% self weight it is 3.8%.

## Change

Sparse-MLA forwards whose inputs require grad additionally write `o_lo = fp32(O) - bf16(O)`, the exact rounding residual of `out` (same shape/dtype as `out`, saved for backward), and the backward preprocess forms `dpsum = rowsum(dO * (out + o_lo))`. `out + o_lo` reproduces the kernel's fp32 accumulator to ~2^-17. `out`/`lse` are bitwise unchanged; composes with `gather_bwd_recompute_p` and `gather_bwd_token_chunk`; no user-facing knobs. `_flash_attn_fwd` returns a 5th value (`o_lo`); `_flash_attn_bwd_sparse_mla` / `_bwd_preprocess` take an optional `o_lo` and behave exactly as before when it is `None`.

Why a residual rather than an fp32 output or a recompute: dpsum needs `dO`, which only exists in the backward, so the fp32 `O` has to cross the fwd/bwd boundary; a bf16 residual costs the same as `o_lo` would in fp32 while the model keeps consuming a bf16 `out`, and recomputing `O` in the backward would be another full P·V pass.

Both kernels sit at their register cap, so the naive implementations spilled badly (+8 ms). The shipped versions re-read the fp32 O from TMEM per 32-column chunk after the O TMA store (the `correction_rescale` access pattern) and stream the preprocess one row-slice at a time when a residual is present; the original preprocess path is untouched when no residual is passed.

## Accuracy

T = S = 4096, W = 2048, H = 128, bf16, fp64 reference from the same bf16 inputs, rel-L2 in absolute units (1.66e-3 = the bf16 output-rounding floor). "Before" is the previous PR (exact max, dpsum from the bf16 output). FlashMLA fwd + cuDNN-frontend 1.29 DSA bwd on bit-identical inputs is shown as a reference; it can only form dpsum from FlashMLA's bf16 output. Peaked inputs put the dominant key in slot 0 (top-k order).

| inputs (median self weight) | pipeline | dq | dqv | dk | dv |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| peaked (0.17) | before | 3.18e-3 | 3.10e-3 | 2.67e-3 | 1.85e-3 |
| peaked (0.17) | **after** | **2.39e-3** | **2.35e-3** | **1.70e-3** | **1.61e-3** |
| peaked (0.17) | FlashMLA + cuDNN 1.29 | 3.15e-3 | 3.08e-3 | 3.11e-3 | 2.48e-3 |
| very peaked (0.98) | before | 3.80e-2 | 3.79e-2 | 3.74e-2 | 2.07e-3 |
| very peaked (0.98) | **after** | **2.37e-3** | **2.36e-3** | **1.66e-3** | **1.16e-3** |
| very peaked (0.98) | FlashMLA + cuDNN 1.29 | 3.80e-2 | 3.79e-2 | 3.74e-2 | 2.65e-3 |
| iid (0.00) | before | 2.80e-3 | 2.48e-3 | 2.27e-3 | 2.15e-3 |
| iid (0.00) | after | 2.73e-3 | 2.43e-3 | 2.20e-3 | 2.11e-3 |
| iid (0.00) | FlashMLA + cuDNN 1.29 | 2.44e-3 | 2.21e-3 | 2.44e-3 | 2.39e-3 |
| any | ideal bf16 floor (output rounding only) | 1.66e-3 | 1.66e-3 | – | – |

The very-peaked "before" and the cuDNN pipeline agree to three digits because both form dpsum from bf16 O; the dq norm is inflated by +7.4e-4 relative in both, +2e-5 after. Per-row tails (from the decomposition, ~80% self weight): dq p99 / p99.9 row error 105% / 333% before, 0.44% / 0.90% after. On iid inputs the term is small (dq 2.80e-3 → 2.73e-3; the remaining gap to the cuDNN pipeline's 2.44e-3 is load-P's bf16 saved P, which `gather_bwd_recompute_p=True` removes: 2.36e-3).

## Cost

GB200, T = S = 16K, W = 2048, H = 128, load-P, CUDA-event timing, same GPU back-to-back (mean of 2 runs):

| | fwd (train) ms | bwd ms | fwd+bwd ms | peak extra GiB | saved activations GiB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 9.05 | 33.05 | 40.81 | 20.55 | 12.53 |
| after | 9.73 (+7.5%) | 32.54 (−1.5%) | 41.38 (+1.4%) | 22.55 (+2.0) | 14.53 (+2.0) |

The +2.0 GiB is one `out`-sized bf16 tensor (16K × 128 heads × 512 × 2 B); the streamed preprocess is ~0.5 ms faster than the whole-tile one despite reading a third tensor. For scale, the FlashMLA + cuDNN pipeline keeps only `out + lse` between fwd and bwd (2.0 GiB at this size and head count vs 12.5 GiB here, of which the saved bf16 P is 8 GiB and `o_lo` 2 GiB; with `gather_bwd_recompute_p=True` FA4 keeps 4 GiB), and at equal head count FA4's fwd+bwd is ~1.4x faster than that pipeline in a separate benchmark, so the residual's cost does not change the standing of either.

## Tests

- New `test_flash_attn_mla_sparse_bwd_precise_dpsum` (varlen × recompute_p × causal, 8 cases): fp64 reference with an emulated ideal-pipeline calibration, no-residual baseline through the internal entry points, residual semantics (`|o_lo| <= ulp(out)/2`, `out + o_lo` closer to fp64 than `out`), token-chunk composition (dq/dqv bitwise vs unchunked). Passes in fake and real mode.
- All 44 `mla_sparse` tests (36 from the base branches + these 8) pass in fake and real mode.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Token-pair gather for 64-head sparse MLA (fwd + bwd)
body:
Stacked PRs:
 * __->__#2884
 * #2883


--- --- ---

## Human Note

Prototype still of using pack_gqa factor to acutally run mutliple queries+heads and stop wasting all our compute. we have to union of the topk list so  the perf is data dependent

## Agent Notes

Two 64-head tokens share a 128-row cluster tile (the kernel's existing 2-tokens-per-tile pack-GQA case, so no padding) and one gather list. The CTA rank selects the token: `m_idx = 2 * cluster_m_block + cta_rank_in_cluster`, peer `m_idx ^ 1`. The gather pointer for a slot is `max(own, peer)`; the validity bitmask uses the CTA's own list, so its 64 rows are masked to its token's selection with the existing mask path. Causal `seqlen_k_limit` is per token (the gather itself uses the pair max). Forward and backward, non-varlen. H <= 64: fewer heads pad to the 64-row half-tile with #2883's mechanism (each CTA still holds one token, so the per-CTA mask is unchanged); verified at H = 16, 32, 48. 64 < H < 128 stays on the single-token padded tile.

Index contract (`_flash_attn_fwd(..., gather_kv_token_pairs=True)`): rows `2p` and `2p+1` of `gather_kv_indices` hold the same pair-union list, padded to a multiple of 128, with `-1` at the slots that token does not attend. `-1` is the minimum, so `max(own, peer)` recovers the union without a third tensor.

Unchanged: attention math, the 128-head path, tiling, pipeline synchronization, #2883's padding path (still used for other head counts).

## Why it helps

Per token the padded tile does 128 rows x K slots of MMA for 64 useful rows. The pair tile does 128 rows x |A u B| slots, all rows useful. Useful MMA fraction = K / |A u B| instead of 1/2, and the pair's KV rows are gathered once. The tile count also halves, which matters because the forward is latency-limited at 1 CTA/SM (NCU in #2883: tensor pipe 38%, no eligible warp 80% of cycles).

Union size from synthetic DSv4-shaped indices (window 128 + causal compressed top-k 512, T=4096):

| indices | \|A\|+\|B\| | \|A u B\| padded to 128 | useful MMA | gather rows vs per-token |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| random top-k | 764 | 573 | 67% | 67% |
| 80%-local top-k | 764 | 474 | 81% | 53% |

Random picks are the floor; a trained indexer should be far more local (smooth scores across adjacent queries, recency skew, and the 128-slot window overlaps 127/128 by construction). At K/N << 1 (very long sequences) the random union approaches 2K and the gain falls back to the tile-count effect unless the indexer is local or tokens are paired by list similarity.

## Measurement

GB200, B=2, H=64, D_qk=64, D_v=512, T=4096, seqlen_k=4096, top-k 512 over causally valid compressed keys (random picks), `_flash_attn_fwd` medians over CUDA-graph replays, no_grad. Correctness against `tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py::attention_ref` on the original per-token lists (fully masked rows compared as zeros).

| path | slots/token | fwd us | vs reference |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| #2883 padded, one token per tile | 512 | 1374 | OK (max err 1.6e-2, pytorch 3.1e-2) |
| token pair, union per tile | 896 | 1030 | OK; vs padded max diff 7.8e-3 |
| H=32: #2883 padded | 512 | 1377 | OK |
| H=32: pad to 64 + token pair | 896 | 1024 | OK; vs padded max diff 7.8e-3 |

`agent_space/token_pairs_probe.py` in the worktree builds the pair-union indices (`pair_union_indices`: sort, unique, membership) and runs both paths.

## Experiment: real DeepSeek-V4-Flash indices

The synthetic tables above assume how much nearby tokens' top-k lists overlap. We measured this with
PG-19 books and concatenated PyTorch source, 32k–256k tokens each. We ran the released
`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, layers 0–2 only, using its reference `inference/model.py`. We checked
that the chunked indexer matched the unchunked reference bit-exactly. We saved the layer-2
lightning-indexer output: each token's list of `index_topk = 512` compressed-KV slots (compress ratio 4).
We passed these lists unchanged to `bench.py --real`: a 4096-token window at each position, H=64,
D=64/512, gathering from the full compressed KV. We compared the padded #2883 path with this PR's pair
path, using CUDA-graph medians on GB200.

![Real V4-Flash indexer: neighbour overlap and pair-union width vs document position](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f640b73e-d448-4541-88e4-b91e86ed0a10)

Left: how many of token t's 512 picks token t+1 also picks, as a fraction. This falls from 0.8 early
in a document to 0.5 at 256k. Right: the width of each pair's union. A typical pair needs 600–770 slots.
But the kernel runs every tile at the widest pair's width in the call
(`n_block_max = topk_length // tile_n`). That width reaches 2K from ~32k tokens on in prose and ~128k
in code.

![Speedup of token pairs over padding with real indices, forward and forward+backward](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/50773ea6-e745-4208-8fc2-64fc638c2fe9)

Forward: pairs are 10–40% faster at every position. Forward+backward: pairs are 11–18% faster while the
widest pair stays under ~900 slots (through 8k in prose, 32k in code). They are 10–15% slower once one
pair pushes the call width to 2K. This is because P/dS and the backward gathers scale with that width.

![Pair speedup vs kernel union width, synthetic and real](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/690428d8-d1bc-4542-a51c-e954ffb541a4)

Synthetic (K=1024) and real (K=512) runs follow one curve when plotted against union-width/K. The gain
depends on the width the kernel runs, not the average overlap. The follow-up to make long-context rows
faster: set `n_block_max` per tile using each token's valid count. This skips each pair's trailing
all-`-1` blocks in the forward, backward main and dQ/dQv/dK kernels. The typical pair's 1.2–1.5x width
predicts ~1.1–1.3x forward+backward everywhere. We also tested 4x32 / 8x16 tiles for H=32 / 16 on these
lists. They are no faster than the padded path: the union grows faster than the rows saved. So these
tiles are not planned.

Harness and data: `agent_space/realistic/` (`samplers.py`, `bench.py`, `plots.py`, `v4flash/run_indexer.py`,
saved lists in `v4flash/indices/*.pt`).

## Not done

- Per-pair variable length instead of padding to the worst pair; varlen; n-way tiles for H < 64.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Support 1..128 Q heads in sparse MLA via in-kernel TMA padding
body:
Stacked PRs:
 * #2884
 * __->__#2883


--- --- ---

## Human Note

Support [1, 128] Q heads in the public sparse MLA (DSA) forward and backward paths. I saw that there was a comment for supporting n_qheads = 64 not sure if you planned to do something fancier here. I did the easy thing (just pad out).  This does infact come up both for dsv4 flash and when doing tp sharding. I found this when trying to integrate into torchtitan. I consider this a naive unblock but it does help :)


I thought about the multi tokens e.g. true pack-gqa but didnt want to visit the union + masking (although ill prototype this) -> same reason why I didnt support this for blocksparse impl

## Agent Notes
TMA pads heads inside the kernel without padded operand copies in global memory. This enables training with 64-head models and tensor-parallel shards.

Each forward tile still covers one token and one top-k gather list: 2-CTA UMMA, 128 packed Q heads, 64 rows per CTA, with K/V split across the pair. Backward uses a 64- or 128-head tile. The dQ/dQv GEMM keeps its 128-row tile with a dynamic head extent.

Unchanged: attention math, the 128-head TMA path, MMA tile sizes, and pipeline synchronization.

### Mechanism

- `padded_qheads_tma_source` builds a heads-first view `(h, d, s, b)` with a dynamic head extent, so CuTe tiles it without requiring divisibility. TMA zero-fills out-of-bounds loads and drops out-of-bounds stores. `regroup_padded_qheads` restores the packed coordinate layout `((tile, s), d, 1, b)`.
- LSE, row_max, and learnable-sink accesses guard the packed head index. Without guards, the hierarchical packed layout wraps padded heads into the next token.
- TMA loads zero padded Q rows in forward and dO/P rows in backward. These rows produce `dS = 0` and contribute nothing to dK/dV. Only `scaleP`/`dPsum` need tile-width global buffers with finite padding.

### Two latent bugs

1. **Backward dV staging at `tile_m=64`.** The split-0 epilogue could overwrite dOt/Qvt operands still used by the split-1 MMA, producing NaNs in `dV[:, 256:]`. If staging equals one operand stage, each split now stages in place over its consumed stage. Otherwise, both splits take turns using one staging area allocated after the operands.
2. **Non-power-of-two preprocess tiles.** A 48-row tile (2 tokens × 24 heads) produced incorrect `dpsum`. Padded head counts now use trivial packing (`qhead_per_kvhead=1, nheads_kv=H`) with the existing 128-row tile. Not all head counts divide that tile; resizing it to a non-power-of-two is not a valid workaround.

### Validation (GB200)

- Sentinel-focused run: 44 passed. `test_flash_attn_mla_sparse_bwd_sentinel` covers H ∈ {128, 64, 96, 24, 1} × shared_kv × causal × 2 lengths.
- `test_flash_attn_mla_absorbed`: 96 BF16 cases passed for `1024-1024` and `255-1025`, including the 128-head path.
- Probe against global-memory padding to 128 heads, H ∈ {1, 8, 16, 24, 48, 64, 72, 96, 100, 120}: out/LSE/P/row_max/dQ/dQv bit-identical; dK/dV within 1e-5.

### Performance at DeepSeek-V4 shapes

Measurement contract: GB200, B=1, D_qk = D_v = 512, shared KV, sliding window 128 + compressed causal top-k, via attention-gym `selected_attention`. Flash uses top-k 512; pro uses top-k 1024. Times are medians over CUDA-graph replays, in µs per call (lower is better). Peak memory is MB (lower is better).

Calculated rates (higher is better): fwd FLOPs = 2*T*H*K*(D_qk + D_v), K = valid gathered slots (top-k + window); bwd FLOPs = 2.5× fwd. TB/s counts gathered KV rows plus Q read and O write.

| T | config | fwd us | fwd TFLOPS | fwd TB/s | bwd us | bwd TFLOPS | fwd+bwd us | peak MB |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 859 | 400 | 3.75 | 1874 | 458 | 2733 | 2114 |
| 4096 | flash H=64 gmem pad->128 | 1061 | 324 | 3.04 | 2835 | 303 | 3896 | 4557 |
| 4096 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 918 | 749 | 4.10 | 2465 | 697 | 3382 | 4046 |
| 4096 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 1349 | 917 | 4.38 | 3798 | 814 | 5147 | 5109 |
| 8192 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 1666 | 412 | 3.87 | 3702 | 464 | 5368 | 4095 |
| 8192 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 1775 | 774 | 4.24 | 4876 | 705 | 6651 | 7959 |
| 8192 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 2650 | 933 | 4.46 | 7539 | 820 | 10189 | 10087 |
| 16384 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 3293 | 417 | 3.91 | 7347 | 468 | 10640 | 8061 |
| 16384 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 3506 | 784 | 4.29 | 9723 | 707 | 13229 | 15789 |
| 16384 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 5262 | 940 | 4.49 | 15029 | 823 | 20292 | 20045 |

At T=4096, H=64 in-kernel padding reduces fwd+bwd time by about 30% and peak memory by about half versus global-memory padding. H=64 forward takes about 93% of the H=128 time. NCU on the H=64 forward (T=4096): DRAM throughput 8%, L2 hit rate 74%, 74% of stall cycles are long-scoreboard waits on the per-thread cp.async gather. The forward is gather-latency-bound, so the padded MMA rows cost little; the gather itself is the lever for a follow-up.

Separate T=2048 comparison: GB200, top-k 512, D=512, fwd+bwd via attention-gym `selected_attention`; time in µs per call (lower is better).

| Configuration | fwd+bwd us |
|---|---:|
| H=64 in-kernel padding | 1416 |
| Native H=128 | 1740 |
| H=64 gmem padding to 128 | 1979 |

title: One more deprecation;
Numeric tweaks to fp8
body:
Numeric tweaks to fp8 rescale and offset

Addressing: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/issues/2577 

This however has some tradeoffs ill show. And this is choice is not yet finalized;

## Summary

The summary in that issue is pretty much spot on and I agree with its fix although there is some interesting perf/ numeric trade offs, and fundamentally the optimal choice is data dependent so we might wanna think about exposing this somehow.

TLDR: With `offset=8` and `rescale_threshold=4`, the max intermediate value in the first `P` block is `2^8 = 256`. A later block can have an unshifted max up to 3.999 log2 units above the tracked max. Because this increase is below the threshold, we keep the old `M` and skip rescaling the accumulator. The second block's max intermediate `P` value can then approach `2^(8+4) = 4096`.

This exceeds E4M3's max value of 448. The denominator `l_i` is accumulated in FP32, but `P` is cast to E4M3 before `P @ V`, causing these large values to saturate. The denominator includes the original values while the numerator includes only their clipped contributions. Final normalization therefore can destroy these values that should contribute to the output

lets say we set rescale threshold to zero,  then any increase in the block max also updates `M`. The  previous accumulator and `l_i` are rescaled by `alpha = 2^(M_old - M_new)`, and the new block is evaluated relative to `M_new`. Its max intermediate `P` value is therefore `2^8 = 256`, rather than 4096.

The current Pr uses a threshold of `0.75`; it allows the maximum to reach `2^8.75 ≈ 431`, which remains below 448, while still avoiding some accumulator rescales, but there are many ways to accomplish the same affect


### Perf Numeric Summary

-- agent notes -- 

#### Pareto frontier

![E4M3 offset-threshold Pareto](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drisspg/flash-attention/8690cd53d13f7c6de766ff2814068d051adb70a6/issue2577/pareto-overview.png)

The full confirmation supports **`max_offset=8, rescale_threshold=0`** as the best global policy measured. Relative to upstream `(4,4)`:

| Path | Median latency | Time-weighted latency | Median relative-L2 / upstream |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Production decode, auto-SplitKV | +0.11% | +0.01% | 0.9945 |
| Decode diagnostic, forced one split | +0.94% | +0.94% | 0.8917 |
| Paged causal prefill | -2.70% | -3.80% | 0.9382 |

Lower is better. Threshold zero produced the stable prefill improvement. Offsets 6–8 had no reproducible performance ordering in the focused recheck, so offset 8 is preferred for its wider retained probability-tail range and slightly better aggregate prefill numerics. The tradeoff is roughly 1% slower forced-one-split decode; production auto-SplitKV decode remained neutral.

> **Implementation note:** the current diff uses `(8, 0)` for FP8 inputs, matching the measured global policy.

#### Why `(8, 0)` vs `(8, 0.75)`

`0.75` does genuinely help decode: it skips accumulator corrections when the running maximum increases by less than the threshold. Relative to `(8,0)`, `(8,0.75)` was **0.12% faster time-weighted** across the broad 72-case auto-SplitKV decode set and **0.61% faster** across the 72 forced-one-split cases. In a focused two-case long-context recheck, the gains were larger—**1.67%** and **4.26%**, respectively—showing that correction cost can be exposed in long unsplit decode.

Threshold zero, however, is a distinct compile-time specialization that removes the positive-threshold compare/select sequence. A codegen isolation test compared `0` with `1e-6`: their BF16 outputs matched bit-for-bit in **8/8** cases, but `1e-6` was **7.66% slower time-weighted** for prefill. `0.75` recovered some work by skipping real corrections, but remained **6.24% slower** than zero for prefill. It also had slightly worse aggregate numerics than zero.

I am going to stick with (8, 0) for now but int eh future this should maybe be user configurable .. 

#### Methodology

- **Discovery:** 38 distinct offset/threshold pairs, 54 matched cases each — **2,052 cells**.
- **Confirmation:** 9 selected pairs, 216 matched cases each — **1,944 cells**.
- **Focused recheck:** 5 finalists across 8 long-context cases with rotated policy order — **40 cells**.
- **Total:** **4,036 matched policy/workload cells**.
- Captured Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B attention tensors using C4 and instruction/GSM8K text, layers 0/16/27, and realistic MHA/GQA geometry.
- Paged causal decode used `Q=1`, `SK={129,512,2048,8192}`, both auto-SplitKV and forced one split. Paged causal prefill used `Q=K`, `S={512,2048,4096,8192}`.
- NVIDIA B200 with SM clock locked to 1500 MHz. Warm fixed-pointer CUDA-graph timing; quantization/setup excluded.
- Numerics compare FA4 against FP32 attention over the exact dequantized vLLM-style E4M3 inputs. This measures isolated FA4 attention, not end-to-end vLLM serving.

<details>
<summary>Full 2D discovery heatmaps</summary>

Green is better than upstream `(4,4)`. Unsafe pairs are retained as diagnostic controls and show the expected rapid saturation.

![E4M3 offset-threshold heatmaps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drisspg/flash-attention/8690cd53d13f7c6de766ff2814068d051adb70a6/issue2577/pair-grid-heatmaps.png)

</details>

## E5M2 follow-up

![E5M2 offset-threshold Pareto](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drisspg/flash-attention/773da26c7381359ee09b1983759dfdd4c88f5d47/issue2577/e5m2-pareto-overview.png)

I repeated the performance/numerics sweep with the captured inputs quantized to E5M2. This supports retaining `max_offset=8` and changing E5M2 from `rescale_threshold=4` to **`rescale_threshold=0`**. Relative to inherited `(8,4)`:

| Path | Median latency | Time-weighted latency | Median relative-L2 / `(8,4)` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Production decode, auto-SplitKV | -0.52% | -0.55% | 1.0000 |
| Decode diagnostic, forced one split | +0.08% | +0.11% | 0.9191 |
| Paged causal prefill | -3.49% | -4.17% | 0.9270 |

Threshold zero again removes the positive-threshold compare/select path and improves prefill while remaining slightly faster for production auto-SplitKV decode. A focused 8K forced-one-split decode recheck exposed the path-specific downside more clearly: `(8,0)` was about **3.1% slower** than `(8,4)` there.

E5M2's extra exponent range is still being used at offset 8: its effective probability floor is `2^-24`, versus `2^-17` for E4M3 at the same offset. Threshold-zero offsets 8, 12, and 15 produced essentially identical numerics, so spending more saturation headroom on a larger offset did not help. The grid did not test offsets below 8; this supports retaining the existing offset, not claiming that 8 is the global E5M2 optimum for every context length.

#### E5M2 methodology

- **Discovery:** 40 pairs (34 safe candidates plus 6 saturation controls) × 54 cases — **2,160 cells**.
- **Confirmation:** 8 selected pairs × 216 cases — **1,728 cells**.
- **Focused recheck:** 6 policies × 8 long-context cases — **48 cells**.
- **Total:** **3,936 matched policy/workload cells**.
- Same Qwen2.5-1.5B/Qwen2.5-7B captures, prefill/decode shapes, B200 timing contract, and FP32-reference methodology as the E4M3 study; only the input quantization format changed to E5M2.

<details>
<summary>Full E5M2 2D discovery heatmaps</summary>

![E5M2 offset-threshold heatmaps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drisspg/flash-attention/773da26c7381359ee09b1983759dfdd4c88f5d47/issue2577/e5m2-pair-grid-heatmaps.png)

</details>

title: Add aux-scalars to interface to enable dynamic ints and floats in expressions
body:
Add aux-scalars to interface to enable dynamic ints and floats in expressions

## Summary

Right now we have Aux-tensors mixin data coming from global tensors,

This pr provides the same functionality but for scalar values via  `aux_scalars`. 

With this we can write mask/score mods that are dynamic over python ints and floats instead of needing to recompute. The most common case is for decode attention. Today that is done via 1 off seq_len info but in general this could have been done via generic query and key size or a dynamic integer offset ( handy if you cant derive from input tensor sizes).

### Examples

```Python
   @cute.jit
   def shifted_causal_mask(batch, head, q_idx, kv_idx, seqlen_info, aux_tensors, aux_scalars):
       q_offset = cutlass.Int32(aux_scalars[0])
       return kv_idx <= q_idx + q_offset


   out = flash_attn_func(
       q,
       k,
       v,
       mask_mod=shifted_causal_mask,
       aux_scalars=[cutlass.Int32(cache_position)],
   )
  ```


I have the PyTorch PR here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/186019
This removes the largest coverage gap between triton and flex/flash :)


## Review guidance

I can merge the two in to an AuxStruct if we want to reduce the number of kwargs for internal kernel funcs -> down for whatever

# CLC Scheduler Heuristic

Human note: I had Pi summarize all the things we ran. We pair-wrote compile + run scripts around the benchmark helper from Inductor / transformer-nuggets that flushes L2 and returns sample statistics, then bootstrapped a paired 95% confidence interval around `speedup_on_vs_off`.

## Shipped heuristic

Disable CLC (use **STATIC** scheduling) when either:

1. **varlen MHA** — varlen with `q_heads == kv_heads`
2. **dense noncausal** — non-varlen, non-causal, non-local-windowed

Otherwise, keep the CLC path available.

## Decision metric

All comparisons use:

- **`speedup_on_vs_off`**
- paired **95% confidence interval**
- significance flag **`ci95_excludes_1x`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `speedup_on_vs_off > 1.0` | CLC is faster |
| `speedup_on_vs_off < 1.0` | CLC is slower |
| `ci95_excludes_1x = True` | difference is statistically stable |


## Aggregate summary by workload

| Workload | Cases | Significant | Wins | Losses |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dense | 750 | 693 | 324 | 369 |
| Varlen | 7200 | 5353 | 3674 | 1679 |
| Block-sparse | 1872 | 878 | 427 | 451 |

## Dense

### Aggregate result

| Cases | Significant | Wins | Losses | Mean Δ% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 750 | 693 | 324 | 369 | +5.74 |

Dense is mixed overall, but the shipped heuristic explicitly gates the dense noncausal bucket.

### Dense by causal

| Setting | Cases | Significant | Wins | Losses | Mean Δ% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal | 375 | 357 | 257 | 100 | +14.02 |
| Noncausal | 375 | 336 | 67 | 269 | -2.53 |

**Dense causal is a strong net win (+14.02%), while dense noncausal is a net regression (-2.53%).** The mixed aggregate (+5.74%) is the average of a very positive causal story and a clearly negative noncausal one.

### Dense by head mode

| Mode | Cases | Significant | Wins | Losses | Mean Δ% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `mha` | 150 | 149 | 67 | 82 | +3.75 |
| `gqa2` | 150 | 135 | 56 | 79 | +4.32 |
| `gqa4` | 150 | 132 | 59 | 73 | +5.43 |
| `gqa8` | 150 | 137 | 65 | 72 | +6.54 |
| `mqa` | 150 | 140 | 77 | 63 | +8.69 |

All dense head modes are net positive in mean Δ%, but all have significant losses. MQA is the strongest positive; MHA is weakest but still positive because dense causal MHA wins dominate.

### Representative dense slowdowns with raw latency / TFLOPS

These rows were rerun in isolation in the **nightly** env using the same nuggets stats path as the main profile flow.

| Case | off us | on us | off TFLOPS | on TFLOPS | Δ% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `mha_noncausal_q16384_k8192_h128` | 1341.76 | 1506.55 | 1638.9 | 1459.6 | -10.94 |
| `mha_noncausal_q4096_k8192_h128` | 681.61 | 692.48 | 1613.1 | 1587.8 | -1.57 |
| `mha_noncausal_q8192_k16384_h96` | 1239.74 | 1256.44 | 1330.3 | 1312.7 | -1.33 |
| `mha_noncausal_h128_16k` | 2800.41 | 3058.16 | 1570.5 | 1438.1 | -8.43 |
| `mha_noncausal_h128_8k` | 1349.75 | 1492.85 | 1629.2 | 1473.0 | -9.59 |

Takeaway: the isolated nightly reruns still show real dense noncausal MHA regressions, but the exact magnitude varies by shape. The strongest quoted regressions remain in the long h128 cases.

### Representative dense wins

These rows were also rerun in isolation in the **nightly** env using the nuggets stats path.

| Case | off us | on us | off TFLOPS | on TFLOPS | Δ% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `mqa_causal_q16384_k1024_h64` | 84.93 | 46.13 | 809.2 | 1489.8 | +84.11 |
| `mqa_causal_q16384_k1024_h96` | 91.12 | 52.72 | 1131.2 | 1955.1 | +72.83 |
| `gqa8_causal_q16384_k1024_h64` | 84.97 | 49.93 | 808.7 | 1376.4 | +70.19 |
| `mqa_causal_q8192_k1024_h64` | 89.07 | 52.18 | 771.5 | 1316.9 | +70.69 |

### Dense tree fit

To avoid learning a recompilation-dependent rule, this tree was refit **without sequence-length features**.

Features used:

- `is_mha`
- `q_per_kv`
- `d`
- `is_causal`

Strict label:

- **class: 1** = enable CLC
- **class: 0** = do not enable CLC from this strict label
- enable iff `ci95_excludes_1x and speedup_on_vs_off > 1.0`

```text
|--- is_causal <= 0.50

|   |   |--- class: 0
|   |--- d >  80.00
|   |   |--- class: 0
|--- is_causal >  0.50
```

## Varlen

title: Deterministic backward for blocksparse impl
body: Stacked PRs: * #2512 * __->__#2253 --- --- --- # Deterministic backward for blocksparse impl PyTorch PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/174813 ## Summary This make it possible to run bwd with blocksparse tensors w/ determinism. At a very high level, the current implementation needs two things 1. For every M x N block, a way to figure out for N_i is it this columns turn to accumulate DQ into the global memory. For dense it can infer this by predefined sparsity, I.e. dense, causal, sliding window. 2. Some coordination with the tile schedule to ensure that we throws work tiles in the queue in a way that will not block any given row from making progress. This is a fun little problem and I made some animations: https://x.com/drisspg/status/2022438130893426731?s=20 But that being said I feel as though there are two approaches for block sparsity, we could either compute the semaphore lock value for every N tile at runtime based off of the sparse data, Or we can precompute the lock values ahead of time. I did not go with approach 1 and went with approach 2 because in terms of total work, since sparsity is typically consistent across layers we get to amortize the construction and I was concerned that doing the scan across kv_blocks and indices would be too much overhead. ### So what does this look like We introduced 3 new attributes to `BlockSparseTensors` ( I wish this was 2 but we will come back to this): New dq_write_order(partial|full) mirroring the q_block_idx(num_blocks) tensors. They are used as such: ```Py dq_write_order: int32[B, H, num_n_blocks, max_q_per_n] ``` Parallel to `q_block_idx[B, H, num_n_blocks, max_q_per_n]`. Each KV column worker iterates from 0 to max_q_per_n, so for the i-th M-block in the CTA's iteration list: ```Py m_block = q_block_idx[b, h, n_block, i] my_lock_value = dq_write_order[b, h, n_block, i] ``` If we we can figure out via the total counts whether I corresponds to partial or full block and thats basically it. See animation :) ### Scheduling I implemented this and perf was terrible since by default we would use the `non-spt` path. SPT is fancy word for right to left. `spt=shortest processing time` for most causal masks they look lower triangular which means the amount of work for a column is highest on the left, since q_idx = 0 which is >= to all kv_indices and thus all m_blocks will contribute - and smallest on the right since the only block that has any actual dQ to compute is the last block for Nth columns iteration. ``` n_block (KV) 0 1 2 3 4 ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ 0 │ ██ │ │ │ │ │ ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 1 │ ██ │ ██ │ │ │ │ m ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ (Q) 2 │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ │ │ ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 3 │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ │ ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 4 │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ ██ │ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ work: 5 4 3 2 1 ``` Bad scheduling is terrible for perf, you turn beautiful parallel GPU into terrible serialized turtle. So I also add 1 more flag which is SPT. And that says in stead of scheduling using the default left to right flip the lock values so that go from lowest to highest from right left. This does require coordination with the scheduler. Why? Again lets look at causal for simplicity - Lets say your num_sms was 2 and your total KV blocks was 5 if you did the default scheduling we would throw work into the queue starting with kv_block 0 and kv_block 1 for m_tile 0 we would be good for m_tile 1 we would also be good since there is their lock values are 0 and then 1,0 but for m_row 2 we would have lock values (2, 1) and semaphore value 0 is at kv_block 2! So our workers will never be able to continue ``` n_block 0 1 2 3 4 ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ 0 │ 0 │ │ │ │ │ ✓ only CTA 0, lock=0 ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 1 │ 1 │ 0 │ │ │ │ ✓ CTA 1 lock=0 goes first, then CTA 0 m ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ (Q) 2 │ 2 │ 1 │ 0 │ │ │ ✗ lock=0 is at n_block=2 — not running! ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 3 │ 3 │ 2 │ 1 │ 0 │ │ ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤ 4 │ 4 │ 3 │ 2 │ 1 │ 0 │ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ ``` So long story short with SPT for most causally blocks we are seeing around the 20-30 perf drop from deterministic bwd -> see attached data. ### Better Scheduling I was toiling with ideas for more optimal scheduling. Since the distribution of tiles can be arbitrary for BlockSparse, I think if we could ahead of time compute a `least blocking schedule` and then we use this schedule to submit kv_tiles, again this requires coordination with the scheduler and would probably add some slow down since get_next_tile_info will need a global read to figure out where to go. I think we would need to have 1 lock value per column in order to avoid any deadlocks and I thought of some good heuristics but afaik this is NP complete. Hard to say if all this AOT work would be worth the potentially faster bwd. Sounds like a future problem. Although lets say we did this I do kinda want `spt` attribute to really be `schedule` attribute which can either be non spt, spt or a permutation. Couldnt think of anything really elegant here ** ideas from reviewer welcome**. #### Fuzzing Side note I did a bunch of fuzzing for this PR, one really nice aspect (or not lol) is that the ratio of compile time to gpu work is very high so both testing and fuzzing is very amenable to parallel workers. This fuzzing lead to this PR: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/pull/2258 ### Performance: Sliding window size = 2048 and eventually starts to get majorly blocked This is with SPT = True And here is SPT = False

title: [CuTe, SM100] Preserve hd256 output alignment for vectorized stores
body:
## Summary

Preserve output alignment through the dedicated SM100/SM110 HD256 forward kernel so its epilogue can use vectorized stores.

The output is already physically aligned, but the kernel loses the compiler's stride/pointer alignment information when creating its view and applying a packed-query offset. In the diagnosed 512-token prefill specialization this scalarized the output stores (`STG.E.U16` instead of `STG.E.128`).

- Use the existing `assume_tensor_aligned` helper for the output view.
- Use the existing `domain_offset_aligned` helper for the cumulative-query row offset.
- First zero dynamic strides on singleton output axes. PyTorch considers tensors with arbitrary unused singleton strides contiguous, so the existing output validator accepts them; asserting divisibility on those raw strides would be incorrect. This normalization changes only the kernel's view, not the caller's tensor, accepted layouts, cache signature, or storage.

Attention math, tiling, pipeline synchronization, and backward kernels are unchanged. No new package dependency.

## Safety and coverage

Adds 14 cases covering FP16/BF16, paged and packed KV, padded/transposed outputs, minimally 16-byte-aligned storage offsets, nonzero cumulative-Q offsets, and singleton batch/sequence/head strides. The tests compare against independent FP64 math attention with low-precision math attention as the error baseline, check finite outputs, and verify that output guards and caller strides are preserved.

For nonsingleton axes, the existing output validator guarantees 16-byte-aligned strides. A cumulative-Q offset moves by whole rows, preserving that alignment. For singleton axes, the normalized stride is zero before the alignment assumption. Static strides receive no new divisibility assumptions.

These are layout-safety tests, not timing assertions; the original implementation is numerically correct on these fixtures too. The performance regression is demonstrated separately below.

## Performance

GPU time per **forward attention call**, in microseconds; lower is better. Speedup is parent time / patched time. Baseline: `0f3fb00d3f34196ca55f30d2f6c5dce0709b4667`.

| Workload | Parent (µs) | Patched (µs) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Decode, batch 1, Q=1, KV=512 | 11.45 | 11.03 | 1.04× |
| Decode, batch 1, Q=1, KV=4096 | 40.77 | 40.32 | 1.01× |
| Decode, batch 8, Q=1, KV=4096 | 91.17 | 90.26 | 1.01× |
| Prefill, batch 1, Q=KV=128 | 40.71 | 9.61 | 4.24× |
| Prefill, batch 1, Q=KV=512 | 44.58 | 13.12 | 3.40× |
| Chunked prefill, batch 4, Q=128, KV=4096 | 80.33 | 50.85 | 1.58× |
| Prefill, batch 1, Q=KV=4096 | 245.12 | 116.54 | 2.10× |
| Ragged batch 2, Q=[129,513], KV=[257,1025] | 52.52 | 19.25 | 2.73× |

Measurement contract:
- GB300/SM103, BF16, GQA 16 query heads / 4 KV heads, head dimension 256, causal, 128-token KV pages, packed K/V cache strides, preallocated output, LSE enabled on both sides.
- PyTorch `2.15.0.dev20260909+cu132`, CUTLASS DSL `4.6.2`, Quack `0.6.4`, TVM-FFI `0.1.12`, Triton `3.8.0+gitc01b6774`.
- Same process, GPU, inputs, launch path, and dependencies; separate JIT caches and parent/patched kernel classes. Seed 42, normal-random BF16 inputs, shuffled page mappings.
- CUDA graph containing 32 calls with fixed warm/reused buffers; 25 warmup batches, 100 replay samples, three interleaved rounds (before/after, after/before, before/after), median of round medians. Native clocks/DVFS; telemetry recorded. No locked-clock or cold-DRAM claim.
- Uses Transformer Nuggets' CUDA-graph benchmark helper. Excludes compilation, graph capture, cache updates, model projections, and scheduling. Not an end-to-end model throughput result. Backward performance was not measured because the patch does not touch backward.
- Both implementations passed FP64/low-precision reference checks and produced bitwise-identical outputs for all eight measured workloads.

## Validation

- 14 new output-layout cases passed on GB300.
- 13 existing HD256 layout/paged-KV cases passed.
- Compute Sanitizer memcheck on all seven new BF16 cases: **0 errors**.
- Eight before/after benchmark workloads passed their reference and bitwise-equivalence checks.
- Focused review of the alignment, singleton-stride, and cache-signature contracts found no remaining blocker after the singleton-stride handling was added.
- Repository pre-commit Ruff check/format hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

The full attention suite, SM110 hardware, backward benchmarks, and racecheck were not run. The patch does not address the separate existing NaN-in-unused-V padding behavior.

title: [CuTe, SM100] Dedicated FP8 E4M3 2-CTA forward kernel (1.2-1.9x on B200/GB300)
body:
Dense E4M3 attention with `head_dim = head_dim_v = 256` on Blackwell runs the generic hd256 2-CTA forward kernel, whose BF16-shaped schedule leaves the FP8 tensor cores waiting on softmax and TMEM traffic. This PR adds a dedicated persistent 2-CTA FP8 forward kernel (`flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_forward_fp8.py`) and dispatches to it from `flash_attn_func` for dense `float8_e4m3fn` inputs on SM100 (B200) and SM103 (B300 / GB300). Its BF16 output and FP32 LSE are **bitwise identical** to the generic kernel.

## What the kernel does differently

- persistent static scheduling; causal tiles are ordered longest-first with alternate waves reversed so trip counts balance across the grid;
- separate three-deep K and V TMA rings, one full-D QK^T MMA per KV block, QK^T issued one KV block ahead of PV;
- SM103: `tcgen05.ld.red` returns the row max together with the score tile; SM100 uses a plain TMEM load and a software max (same result, max is exact);
- the online-softmax correction factor is handed to the correction warps through SMEM, and the accumulator rescale is skipped when every factor in the warp is exactly 1.0.

FP32 accumulation, the softmax reduction order, the EX2 emulation settings and the FP8 P conversion are unchanged from the generic kernel, which is why the outputs are bitwise identical.

## Dispatch

`_hd256_fp8_dispatch()` in `interface.py`: dense inputs only (no varlen, paged KV, local window, descales, qv), `float8_e4m3fn`, `head_dim = head_dim_v = 256`, compute capability 10.x. `ld.red` is used when the DSL compile target is the SM103 family. E5M2 and every other configuration keep the existing kernels. Both choices are part of the JIT cache key. There are no shape-dependent tuning knobs: half-D QK^T tiles and a 2-deep KV ring were measured on both parts and were not better.

## Tests (`tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py`)

- `test_flash_attn_fp8_hd256_output`: reference comparison on 8 shapes (unaligned tails, aligned diagonal, `seqlen_q <= 128`, several persistent rounds, rows without valid keys, E5M2 fallback);
- `test_flash_attn_fp8_hd256_matches_generic`: bitwise equality with the generic kernel on 4 shapes x `return_lse`;
- `test_flash_attn_fp8_hd256_dispatch_rule` (CPU), `..._uniform_scores` (analytic output/LSE), `..._preallocated_graph` (strided output, CUDA graph replay with changed inputs).

`test_flash_attn_fp8_hd256*` is added to the GPU CI filter; the B200 CI runner now exercises the new kernel (SM100 path).

## Performance

Method: for each shape, both arms (upstream generic kernel and this PR) run in one process with separate JIT caches; outputs are checked bitwise; each arm is captured as a CUDA graph of N back-to-back `flash_attn_func` calls (N sized to ~20 ms), warmed up, and replayed in interleaved order for 6 rounds; the table reports the median per-call time. title: [CuTe, SM100] Add symmetric D512 forward and backward
body:
Add symmetric head dimension 512 (`d_qk = d_v = 512`) to the SM100 CuTe attention path, including FP16/BF16 forward and backward.

### Implementation and scope

- Fused two-CTA dense forward shares QK and online softmax across all 512 output columns, reusing the SM100 MLA pipeline. Generic forward uses two V256 slices for varlen, paged KV, FP8, local masks, softcap and SplitKV; each slice uses the complete D512 QK dot product.
- Separate TCGEN05 dQ/dK/dV kernels keep the working set within shared-memory/TMEM limits. Accumulation and grouped-query partial reduction use FP32, with head grouping and long noncausal tile ordering for reuse.
- Compact layouts keep batch/token extents dynamic, with runtime maximum lengths and scheduling-aware cache keys. Noncompact layouts retain static specialization. Forward, backward and GQA reduction have disk-cache reload regressions.
- Large GQA reduction counts and indices use Int64 from the first multiplication, avoiding overflow at 2^31 output elements.
- Signed window bounds retain their literal meaning. The latest fix also initializes gradients when a negative bound can exclude an entire output tile: for square sequences, those tiles previously skipped their stores and could leave stale gradients. Added tests use nonzero supplied output buffers so allocator reuse cannot hide missing writes.

FP16/BF16: dense/varlen forward and backward, MHA/GQA/MQA, causal/local masks, softcap, LSE gradients and training with SplitKV forward. FP8 E4M3/E5M2 and paged KV are **forward only**. Deterministic backward, learnable sinks, custom score/mask callbacks, block sparsity and sparse gather/scheduler metadata are outside this implementation. Callers must translate external `-1`-means-unbounded conventions to FA4's `None` convention. Validation is on B200; full-graph `torch.compile` integration is not claimed.

Latest follow-up: `71ff336`, retaining the dynamic-cache contribution in `313d646` and the subsequent fixes in `f502aea` and `bed49db`. The diff contains implementation, regression tests and necessary CI wiring; no reports or binary artifacts.

### Validation at `71ff336`

B200, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, quack-kernels 0.6.4:

- A separately installed wheel passed **402 tests: all 394 D512 regressions plus 8 upstream CI-selected smoke cases**, with no skips. All **54 Python modules** match committed source byte-for-byte; interpreter and imported module paths were checked in the controller and workers.
- **56 signed-window cases** cover FP16/BF16, square/rectangular sequences, MHA/GQA, entirely empty and partially empty output tiles, autograd and supplied nonzero gradient buffers. The previous installed wheel failed three sentinel reproductions; the fix also passed 24 independent cases including ordinary-window controls.
- The suite includes cache reuse across batch/token changes, disk reload, output layouts, FP8/paged/SplitKV, independently packed Q/K plus used lengths and LSE gradients, and four checkpoint/autocast/AdamW regressions. The latter exercise a small attention block, not a complete training stack.
- All four large-index reduction cases executed at or above 2^31 output elements, both across and within batches. These require about 40 GiB of buffers and explicitly skip below 48 GiB free memory.
- Compute Sanitizer **memcheck passed four square signed-window MHA/GQA cases with zero errors**. This is targeted sanitizer validation, not a full-suite sanitizer claim.
- The CI driver now selects the D512 file. Local validation used the workflow's filter and the driver's two-stage plan: fake pass **8 passed / 394 skipped**, execution pass **402 passed**. D512 tests require real values and intentionally skip the fake pass. Local execution used four workers; the workflow's default worker count and triggers are unchanged. This is local validation, not a claim that the upstream GitHub Actions workflow has run.
- Ruff on the added kernels/cache helper and `git diff --check` pass. Existing numerical tolerances were not relaxed; comparisons use FP64 and either fixed tolerances or the upstream input-precision error criterion, with finite-value checks.


title: Fix Windows builds with CUDA 13 and PyTorch 2.15
body:
## Summary

Fix the Windows CUDA build failures reported in #2832.

- Add sm_121 to the default CUDA architectures.
- Generate native sm_121 code with compute_121f on CUDA 12.9+.
- Emit forward-compatible PTX only for architectures supported by the active toolkit.
- Use C++20 with PyTorch 2.15+, while retaining C++17 for older releases.
- Enable MSVC’s conforming preprocessor with /Zc:preprocessor.
- Define _USE_MATH_DEFINES so M_LOG2E is available under MSVC.

These are build-configuration changes only; no attention kernel logic is modified.

## Motivation

CUDA 13.x CCCL headers reject MSVC’s traditional preprocessor. Additionally, PyTorch 2.15 headers use C++20 features, including designated initializers and std::strong_ordering.

On an SM 12.1 GPU, the existing architecture defaults also produce no native sm_121 cubin. Finally, MSVC does not expose M_LOG2E unless _USE_MATH_DEFINES is set.

Before this change, these resulted in:

  - CCCL C1189, requesting /Zc:preprocessor
  - C7555 for C++20 designated initializers
  - C2039 for std::strong_ordering
  - Undefined M_LOG2E
  - No native sm_121 code

## Compatibility

PyTorch releases before 2.15 continue to use C++17. The gencode helper now tracks architectures supported by the detected CUDA version, preventing unsupported architectures from being selected for the forward-compatible PTX target.

## Validation

  Tested on:

  - Windows 11 ARM64
  - MSVC 14.51
  - CUDA 13.4.46
  - PyTorch 2.15 Windows ARM64 headers
  - NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 12.1

Validation performed:

  - Reproduced all reported failures using the previous flags.
  - Compiled CCCL, PyTorch 2.15, and <cmath> headers together using the new flags.
  - Verified native sm_121 output and compute-121 PTX with cuobjdump.
  - Verified host compilation with the new MSVC flags.
  - Checked gencode output for CUDA 11.7, 12.8, 12.9, and 13.4.
  - Ran python -m py_compile setup.py and git diff --check.

  Fixes #2832

title: [CuTe, SM90] Fix wrong dQ in backward for head_dims padded to a non-multiple of 32
body:
## Description

The SM90 CuTe backward sets `hdim_multiple_of = 64 if dKV_swapAB else 16`. With the default (non-swapped) dK/dV layout, head_dim 72/104 therefore round `tile_hdim` up to only 80/112, while interface.py allocates and zeroes `dq_accum` with head_dim rounded to 32 (96/128), and the preprocess/postprocess steps use the same granularity. The kernel never writes the tail of the padded accumulator (columns 80-95 / 112-127), and the postprocess readback carries that stale data into dQ. Forward, dK and dV are unaffected; dQ comes back silently wrong with a uniform four-mismatches-per-column fingerprint.

### Root cause

The kernel-level tiling granularity (16) disagrees with the interface-level allocation granularity (32) for the non-swapped layout.

Use 32 for the non-swapped layout as well, matching the interface allocation. One-line change; a no-op for head_dims that are already multiples of 32, and the swapAB path is unchanged.

## Examples

Repro cell (bf16, seqlen 512, 8 heads, head_dim 72, non-causal, varlen with a single sequence), dQ checked against an fp32 SDPA reference at atol=rtol=0.05:

```python
import torch
from flash_attn.cute.interface import flash_attn_varlen_func

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(512, 8, 72, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda") for _ in range(3))
cu = torch.tensor([0, 512], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
out = flash_attn_varlen_func(q, k, v, cu, cu, 512, 512, causal=False)
dq = torch.autograd.grad(out.float().pow(2).sum(), q, retain_graph=False)[0]
```

Affected head_dims: 72, 80, 104, 112 (16-aligned padding that is not a multiple of 32).

## Performance Data

No performance claim: this is a pure correctness fix. The change only alters tile padding granularity for the affected head_dims and is a no-op for head_dims that are already multiples of 32.

## Verification

A/B on H100 (SM90), bf16 inputs against an fp32 SDPA reference, head_dim in {72, 104} x causal in {False, True}, same seed/shapes/tolerances per cell. The stock build fails all four cells: three return dQ with more than half of all elements mismatched (uniform four-per-column fingerprint; fwd/dK/dV exact), and head_dim 104 non-causal additionally fails to compile with an MLIR partition error. With the patch all four cells pass, and every per-tensor max_abs_diff matches the same cells run on stock B100 (SM100), which does not have the bug. The analogous fix for the swapped layout landed upstream as [#2482](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/pull/2482).

title: [ROCm/CK] Fix num_splits heuristic, which could never return more than 1
body:
Cause
-----
override_num_splits_if_necessary() passed num_splits_heuristic_ck() two wrong inputs, leaving split-KV dead code: num_splits=0 was bit-identical to num_splits=1 on every shape measured.

1. num_n_blocks was ceildiv(hdim_v, kN1) with kN1 = hdim_v, i.e. a constant 1. It counts the KV-sequence blocks a split is carved from, so it must come from seqlen_k, as set_params_splitkv() does on the CUDA side. Pinned at 1, `max_splits = min(max_splits, num_SMs, num_n_blocks)` clamped to 1 and the heuristic could only ever return 1. seqlen_k was not even a parameter.

2. The parallelism term used nhead. The splitkv kernel packs the query heads sharing a KV head into one workgroup, so the grid is batch * nhead_k * num_m_blocks; using nhead overstated parallelism by the GQA ratio and suppressed splitting where it pays most. At a fixed batch*nhead of 4096 the gain from splitting tracks batch*nhead_k: 1.02x at 4096, 1.29x at 256, 1.95x at 128, 3.21x at 64.

Fix
---
Pass seqlen_k and nhead_k through and derive both quantities correctly. num_splits_heuristic_ck() itself is unchanged: given correct inputs its choices match, shape for shape, the best policy found by fitting occupancy- and blocks-per-split-based alternatives against measured optima.

The heuristic is also capped at 8 splits, and the `num_splits <= 128` checks become `<= 8`. The CK splitkv combine kernel only reduces up to 8 splits correctly: on gfx950 with CK c56c6750, num_splits 1..8 match an fp32 reference to ~5e-3 relative error while num_splits >= 9 diverge (rel err 0.28..2.0), independently of batch, seqlen_k and causal. Callers passing more than 8 get an error instead of silently wrong output. Lifting that limit in the combine kernel is left to a separate change; it is what holds the win to ~2.2x rather than ~7x, since 25 of the 93 shapes measured have their optimum above 8.

varlen fwd calls the same helper and is updated identically.

Correctness
-----------
Changing num_splits changes the split-K reduction, so this was checked against a full rebuild of the extension (2413 instances, gfx950, 0 errors) rather than by reasoning about the heuristic alone.

The existing suite carries the strongest signal. test_flash_attn_kvcache is already parametrized over num_splits=[1, 0] and over mha/mqa/gqa, d in {32, 59, 64, 80, 128, 256}, new_kv, paged and non-paged KV, rotary (fraction 0/0.5/1.0, interleaved or not), causal, local, alibi and batch_idx. Because 0 always collapsed to 1, none of those cases had ever reached the split-KV path. They do now:

| test                                   | result        |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| tests/test_flash_attn_ck.py -k kvcache  | 152064 passed |
| tests/test_flash_attn_ck.py -k varlen   | 56774 passed  |

On top of that, against an fp32 reference:

| check                                          | result                 |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| auto path (num_splits=0), 12 decode shapes      | rel err 0.0019..0.0036 |
| every split count 1..8, same shapes             | rel err <= 0.0041      |
| num_splits of 9, 64, 128                        | rejected, not computed |
| varlen vs the dense kernel on identical inputs  | rel err 0.00000        |

The rejection cases are the reason for the 8-split cap. Before this change the API accepted up to 128 and the combine kernel silently produced wrong output above 8; the divergence is abrupt (rel err ~5e-3 at 8, 2.0 at 9) and does not depend on batch, seqlen_k, num_n_blocks or causal.

The cap itself is measured on gfx950 with CK c56c6750 only. Whether other architectures or CK revisions share the same limit is untested here, so it is a named constant rather than something derived.

Performance
-----------
93 decode/short-q shapes on MI350X (gfx950), bf16, d=128, batch 1..128, seqlen_k 1K..128K, GQA ratios 1:1..64:1:

| metric                              | value  |
| ----------------------------------- | ------ |
| geomean speedup                     | 2.16x  |
| max speedup                         | 7.3x   |
| geomean vs best reachable at ns<=8  | 1.030x |
| shapes made slower                  | 0      |

Per shape, from the end-to-end run against the rebuilt extension (`auto` is num_splits=0, the path this patch changes; `ns=1` is the old behaviour):

| batch | seqlen_k | q/kv heads | ns=1     | auto     | speedup | rel err |
| ----- | -------- | ---------- | -------- | -------- | ------- | ------- |
| 2     | 131072   | 64/8       | 6.435 ms | 0.988 ms | 6.51x   | 0.0029  |
| 1     | 65536    | 64/8       | 3.237 ms | 0.519 ms | 6.23x   | 0.0030  |
| 4     | 16384    | 64/1       | 0.801 ms | 0.138 ms | 5.80x   | 0.0027  |
| 1     | 16384    | 64/8       | 0.815 ms | 0.144 ms | 5.66x   | 0.0028  |
| 16    | 16384    | 64/1       | 0.836 ms | 0.154 ms | 5.43x   | 0.0030  |
| 8     | 32768    | 64/8       | 1.655 ms | 0.354 ms | 4.67x   | 0.0036  |
| 4     | 4096     | 64/4       | 0.217 ms | 0.051 ms | 4.27x   | 0.0030  |
| 64    | 4096     | 64/1       | 0.243 ms | 0.076 ms | 3.18x   | 0.0029  |
| 1     | 4096     | 64/64      | 0.225 ms | 0.071 ms | 3.15x   | 0.0035  |
| 16    | 4096     | 64/8       | 0.247 ms | 0.114 ms | 2.17x   | 0.0019  |
| 128   | 1024     | 64/8       | 0.191 ms | 0.191 ms | 1.00x   | 0.0021  |
| 64    | 4096     | 64/8       | 0.322 ms | 0.325 ms | 0.99x   | 0.0035  |

The last two rows are shapes with enough parallelism already; the heuristic correctly leaves them at one split. rel err is against an fp32 reference.

title: [CuTe, SM120] Reject backward configurations that exceed shared memory
body:
SM120 backward with equal head dimensions of 192 requests 115712 bytes of shared memory, exceeding the 101376-byte limit. Forward succeeds, but backward reaches `CUDADialectError(cudaErrorInvalidValue)` during compilation. CUTLASS prints the resource counts separately; they are not in the Python exception.

Check the actual shared-storage declaration before emitting the backward kernel and raise a `ValueError` containing the required bytes, limit, tile, and padded head dimensions. Using the declaration includes P/dS, LSE/dPsum, and alignment padding omitted by the existing, unused `can_implement()` estimate. The change only improves rejection of unsupported configurations; it does not add d192 backward support or change supported kernels.

Validation against upstream `edb5c76ee329b18ed95d1f7ea9aa522a1331ab7d`:

- Actual CuTe shared-storage compilation confirms 115712 bytes for d192 and the new `ValueError`; supported d64, d128, and d192/v128 declarations still compile.
- RTX 5090 / SM120: four rejection tests passed (FP16/BF16 × causal/noncausal), with PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130 and CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2.
- Python syntax checks and `git diff --check` passed.
- In separate fresh baseline/candidate processes, 12 supported cases each passed output and dQ/dK/dV comparison to FP64 (with a same-input, output-dtype-rounded FP32 reference): d64/d64, d128/d128, d192/v128 × FP16/BF16 × causal/noncausal, B1/S128/H2. The d192/d192 case reproduced the original CUDA error and the new descriptive `ValueError`, respectively.

Reproduce the new regression test with:

```sh
pytest -q tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py -k sm120_backward_rejects_smem_overflow
```

Related to #2609, which wires the existing `can_implement()` predicates into the interface. Its SM120 predicate still returns `True` for this d192 configuration because it counts 98304 bytes of Q/K/V/dO tiles but not the complete 115712-byte allocation. This small kernel-local check covers that gap without depending on the broader interface change.

AI-assisted implementation and testing. This is a validation/diagnostic fix, not a performance claim.
